title: Honours and Their Cost: Decorating an ARBiH Formation
sources: Balkan Battlegrounds, Vol. I (CIA, 2002), ARBiH formation organisation and morale
ICTY Halilović Trial Judgment (IT-01-48-T), ARBiH command structure and unit accountability
content:
A decoration is a leadership gesture that spends nothing material and risks a great deal symbolic. For the RBiH leadership, the question of whether to single out one steadfast formation, to issue a broad citation across the regular corps, or to decline altogether amid heavy losses was never simply a matter of recognising service. To name one unit was to imply a ranking of all the others; to honour everyone was to honour no one in particular; to withhold honours when the casualty lists were long could read either as sober restraint or as a leadership that no longer noticed.

The wartime practice of recognition cut against the grain of an army still consolidating its formations. Singling out a regular brigade rewarded discipline and the chain of command, but it could breed resentment among units that had bled equally without the citation, and it raised the awkward question of which formations were being held up as exemplary. A leadership recognising service had to be sure of what it was recognising; the ARBiH's accountability record, examined at the ICTY, is a reminder that not every formation's conduct stood up to scrutiny, and that an honour misplaced is harder to retract than to award.

The ambivalence is structural. The citation that lifts one command's morale lowers another's; the broad gesture that offends no one inspires no one; the refusal that reads as honesty to the leadership reads as coldness to the men who expected acknowledgement. Honours ring hollow amid losses, and they ring loudest when they land on the wrong shoulders.

This is a recurring leadership choice rather than a single decorated event, and the Codex holds the most recent decision; the engine binds the shared families — honour one, honour broadly, or decline — not any particular unit. It moves cohesion and morale, not the front. The honest reading is that for the RBiH leadership a decoration was authorship of who the war's example would be, and that the gesture meant to dignify service could as easily seed the resentment it sought to soothe.
